sections.content: If you are new to real estate wholesaling, one of the first questions you probably have is: how many deals does the average wholesaler close per month? It is a fair question, and the honest answer might surprise you. Most people picture successful wholesalers closing deal after deal every week. The reality is a lot more grounded — and understanding the real numbers will help you set better goals and build a more sustainable business.
The Real Numbers: What Average Wholesalers Actually Close

Based on industry surveys and data from active wholesaling communities, the average wholesaler closes between 1 and 3 deals per month. Part-time wholesalers who are still learning the ropes often close 1 deal every 1 to 2 months. Full-time investors working a structured system typically hit 2 to 4 deals per month. Top performers — those with teams, strong buyer lists, and consistent marketing — can close 5 to 10 or more deals monthly. These ranges vary widely depending on your market, your marketing budget, and how much time you invest each week.
Your first deal is the hardest one you will ever close. After that, the system starts to work for you — not the other way around. — Common wisdom in the wholesaling community
Why Deal Volume Varies So Much

Not all wholesalers are operating in the same conditions. A part-time investor in a small Midwest city working with a $500 monthly marketing budget will have very different results than a full-time team in a high-activity market like [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga) or [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx). Several factors directly impact how many deals you can realistically close in a given month.

items: Marketing budget and channels: Direct mail, cold calling, driving for dollars, and paid ads all generate different lead volumes at different costs per deal.
Market activity: High-volume markets like [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az) see more motivated sellers and larger buyer pools, which speeds up the deal cycle.
Experience level: Beginners spend more time on each deal learning the process. Experienced wholesalers can move faster through every step.
Buyer list size and quality: A strong cash buyer network means you can assign contracts in days instead of weeks.
Deal analysis speed: The faster you can evaluate a deal accurately, the faster you can make confident offers.
Follow-up systems: Most deals do not close on the first contact. Consistent follow-up is where a huge percentage of contracts actually get signed.

sections.content: A Realistic Timeline for New Wholesalers

If you are just getting started, do not measure yourself against a 10-deal-per-month wholesaler who has been in the business for five years. Instead, use this rough timeline as a benchmark. In your first 1 to 3 months, your goal is simply to close your first deal. Many new wholesalers take 60 to 90 days to get their first contract signed and assigned. This is completely normal. By months 3 to 6, with consistent marketing and follow-up, you should be targeting 1 deal per month. By the end of your first year, if you are treating this like a real business, 2 to 3 deals per month is an achievable goal. If you want a deeper look at the entire process from scratch, check out our [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) to build your foundation the right way.

Pro Tip: Track every lead, every offer, and every follow-up in a simple CRM or even a spreadsheet. Most wholesalers who struggle are not sending bad offers — they are just failing to follow up. Studies show that 80% of deals require 5 or more contacts before a seller agrees to move forward.
How Much Money Does Each Deal Make?

Deal volume is only part of the picture. What you earn per deal matters just as much. The average wholesale fee in most U.S. markets ranges from $5,000 to $15,000 per deal. In hot or high-priced markets, assignment fees of $20,000 to $30,000 are not uncommon. A wholesaler closing 2 deals per month at an average fee of $8,000 is earning around $16,000 per month — or roughly $192,000 per year before expenses. That is a strong income, but it requires consistent lead generation, accurate deal analysis, and a reliable buyer network working together.
The Math Behind a Profitable Wholesale Business

Here is a simple example. Say you are spending $2,000 per month on direct mail and generating 20 leads. Of those 20 leads, you might make serious contact with 8 sellers, submit offers on 4 properties, and close 1 deal. That is a 5% lead-to-deal conversion rate, which is actually pretty solid for wholesaling. Your cost per deal is $2,000, and if your assignment fee is $10,000, you keep $8,000 in profit. Scale your marketing to $4,000 per month with the same ratios, and you are closing 2 deals and pocketing $16,000. The key is knowing your numbers cold so you can scale what works.
How to Increase Your Deal Volume Step by Step
Closing more deals each month is not about working harder — it is about building better systems. Here is a practical approach to increasing your monthly deal volume without burning out.

items: Step 1 — Expand your lead sources: Do not rely on just one channel. Combine direct mail with cold calling, text blasting, and driving for dollars to keep your pipeline full from multiple directions.

Step 2 — Analyze deals faster and more accurately: The faster you can tell a good deal from a bad one, the more offers you can make. Use a tool like our [Wholesale Deal Calculator](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to quickly run your numbers and build confidence in your offers.

Step 3 — Build your buyer list before you need it: Start networking with cash buyers at local REIA meetups, through Facebook groups, and on the MLS. A warm buyer list cuts your time-to-close dramatically.

Step 4 — Follow up religiously: Set automated reminders to contact every unsold lead every 3 to 4 weeks. Motivated sellers often are not ready the first time you call — but they might be ready in 60 days.

Step 5 — Learn to analyze deals like a pro: Knowing how to accurately calculate ARV, repair costs, and maximum allowable offer is the difference between profitable deals and costly mistakes. Our [How to Analyze Real Estate Deals guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/how-to-analyze-real-estate-deals) walks you through this process in detail.

Step 6 — Hire help when ready: Once you are consistently closing 2 to 3 deals per month, bringing on a part-time acquisition manager or virtual assistant can help you scale without doubling your workload.

sections.content: What Separates 1-Deal-Per-Month Wholesalers from 5-Deal-Per-Month Wholesalers

The biggest difference between average and high-volume wholesalers is not talent or luck — it is systems and consistency. High performers have documented processes for lead intake, seller follow-up, deal analysis, and buyer communication. They treat wholesaling like a business with repeatable workflows, not a side hustle where they wing it every week. They also invest back into their marketing consistently, even in slow months, which keeps their pipeline from ever going dry. If you can master those two things — systems and consistency — you will naturally climb from the 1-deal range to the 3-to-5-deal range within your first year or two.
The wholesalers closing 5 or more deals a month are not smarter than you. They just have better systems running in the background while they focus on building relationships.

Pro Tip: Set a weekly KPI (Key Performance Indicator) instead of a monthly goal. Track how many seller calls you made, how many offers you submitted, and how many follow-ups you sent each week. Small weekly actions compound into big monthly results.
Setting Realistic Goals for Your Wholesaling Business

The most important mindset shift you can make is to stop comparing your chapter one to someone else's chapter ten. Closing 1 quality deal per month as a beginner is a win. Closing 2 consistent deals per month after six months is excellent progress. Chasing unrealistic numbers too soon leads to frustration and shortcuts — like making bad offers just to stay busy — which can actually hurt your reputation and cost you money. Set goals based on your current resources, track your conversion ratios honestly, and raise the bar gradually as your systems improve.
